cards.q: What is addition polymerisation?
cards.a: Many small unsaturated molecules (monomers, usually alkenes) join together to form one long chain molecule, with no other product.
cards.why: The \(\mathrm{C{=}C}\) double bond in each monomer opens up and forms new single bonds to the neighbouring monomers.

cards.q: Draw the repeating unit of the polymer formed from propene.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of propene: a carbon–carbon double bond with a methyl group on one end.

cards.a: Two carbons joined by a single bond; one carries two H atoms, the other an H and a \(\mathrm{CH_{3}}\). Bonds extend out through the brackets, with \(n\) outside.

answerFigure.alt: Repeating unit of poly(propene): two carbon atoms in square brackets with n; the first carries two hydrogens, the second a hydrogen and a methyl group; end bonds pass through the brackets.

cards.why: The methyl group is a branch: it is not part of the main chain, which is made only from the two carbons of the \(\mathrm{C{=}C}\).

cards.q: Draw the repeating unit of poly(chloroethene) (PVC).

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of chloroethene: a carbon–carbon double bond with a chlorine atom on one carbon.

cards.a: Two carbons in the chain: one with two H atoms, the other with an H and a Cl. Continuation bonds through the brackets, and n.

answerFigure.alt: Repeating unit of poly(chloroethene), PVC: two carbon atoms in square brackets with n; the first carries two hydrogens, the second a hydrogen and a chlorine atom.

cards.why: The repeating unit has the same atoms as the monomer: an addition polymer and its monomer have the same empirical formula.

cards.q: Tetrafluoroethene, \(\mathrm{CF_{2}{=}CF_{2}}\), forms PTFE (used for non-stick pans). Name the polymer and draw its repeating unit.
cards.a: Poly(tetrafluoroethene): two carbons, each carrying two fluorine atoms.

answerFigure.alt: Repeating unit of poly(tetrafluoroethene), PTFE: two carbon atoms in square brackets with n, each carrying two fluorine atoms.

cards.why: Name an addition polymer by putting the monomer’s name in brackets after “poly”.

cards.q: Phenylethene is used to make polystyrene packaging. Draw the repeating unit of poly(phenylethene).

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of phenylethene: a benzene ring carrying a CH=CH2 group.

cards.a: Two carbons in the chain: one with two H atoms, the other with an H and a benzene ring (a phenyl group) as a side group.

answerFigure.alt: Repeating unit of poly(phenylethene): two carbon atoms in square brackets with n; the first has two hydrogens, the second a hydrogen and a benzene ring hanging below it.

cards.why: Only the C=C outside the ring takes part. The benzene ring is unchanged and hangs off the chain.

cards.q: Draw the repeating unit of poly(propenenitrile), made from \(\mathrm{CH_{2}{=}CHCN}\) and used in acrylic fibres for jumpers and blankets.
cards.a: Two chain carbons: one with two H atoms, the other with an H and a \(\mathrm{C{\equiv}N}\) group.

answerFigure.alt: Repeating unit of poly(propenenitrile): two carbon atoms in square brackets with n; the first carries two hydrogens, the second a hydrogen and a CN group.

cards.why: Whatever is attached to the C=C carbons becomes a side group on the chain.

cards.q: This is a section of an addition polymer. How many repeating units are shown, and which monomer was used?

figure.alt: A section of an addition polymer chain: six carbon atoms in a row; alternate carbons carry two hydrogens, and the others carry a hydrogen and a methyl group.

cards.a: Three repeating units; the monomer is propene.

answerFigure.alt: Skeletal formula of propene: a carbon–carbon double bond with a methyl group on one end.

cards.why: Each repeating unit is two chain carbons. Put the \(\mathrm{C{=}C}\) back between those two carbons to get the monomer.

cards.q: This is a section of an addition polymer. Draw its repeating unit and name the monomer.

figure.alt: A section of an addition polymer chain: four carbon atoms in a row, each carrying one hydrogen atom above and one methyl group below.

cards.a: The repeating unit is two carbons, each with one H and one \(\mathrm{CH_{3}}\). The monomer is but-2-ene, \(\mathrm{CH_{3}CH{=}CHCH_{3}}\).

answerFigure.alt: Repeating unit of poly(but-2-ene): two carbon atoms in square brackets with n, each carrying one hydrogen atom and one methyl group.

cards.why: Both chain carbons of each unit carry a methyl group, so the double bond was in the middle of a four-carbon molecule. A common slip is to answer propene.

cards.q: Name the addition polymer made from \(\mathrm{CH_{2}{=}CHCH_{3}}\), and the one made from \(\mathrm{CH_{2}{=}CHCl}\).
cards.a: Poly(propene) and poly(chloroethene).
cards.why: IUPAC naming: poly + the monomer’s name in brackets. PVC is the common name for poly(chloroethene).

cards.q: Explain why poly(alkenes) are unreactive.
cards.a: They are saturated, with only strong, non-polar bonds.
marks: Poly(alkenes) are saturated: the chain has no \(\mathrm{C{=}C}\) bonds left.
They contain only strong \(\mathrm{C{-}C}\) and \(\mathrm{C{-}H}\) bonds.
These bonds are (almost) non-polar, so there is no δ+ site for nucleophiles to attack.

cards.q: Explain the intermolecular forces between poly(ethene) molecules, and why poly(ethene) is a solid even though ethene is a gas.
cards.a: Only van der Waals forces, but very many of them along each long chain.
marks: The chains are non-polar, so the forces between them are van der Waals forces (induced dipole–dipole).
Each chain has thousands of atoms, so there are many more points of contact between molecules than in ethene.
The total van der Waals attraction between chains is much greater, so much more energy is needed to separate them.

cards.q: Give typical uses of PVC, and explain how a plasticiser changes its properties.
cards.a:
Rigid PVC: window frames, drainpipes. Plasticised PVC: electrical cable insulation, flooring, clothing.
Plasticiser molecules sit between the chains, pushing them apart, so the chains slide past each other more easily: the PVC becomes flexible.
cards.why: The plasticiser weakens the intermolecular forces between the polymer chains.

cards.q: True or false: the repeating unit of poly(ethene) contains a \(\mathrm{C{=}C}\) double bond.
cards.a: False. The chain is joined by single bonds only.

answerFigure.alt: Repeating unit of poly(ethene): two carbon atoms, each with two hydrogen atoms, in square brackets with n; a bond from each end carbon passes out through the brackets.

cards.why: The double bond opens up when the monomers join, so the polymer is saturated, like an alkane.

cards.q: What is the atom economy of an addition polymerisation, and why?
cards.a: 100%: the polymer is the only product.
cards.why: Every atom of every monomer ends up in the polymer.

cards.q: Poly(ethene) was discovered by accident in 1933. How has the knowledge of polymers developed since then?
cards.a: Early poly(ethene) was made at very high pressure and had branched chains (low density). Later, catalysts were developed that make unbranched chains at lower pressure, giving stronger, high-density poly(ethene).
cards.why: The same monomer can give polymers with different properties depending on how it is made.

cards.q: What is condensation polymerisation?
cards.a: Monomers with two functional groups join together, and a small molecule (usually \(\mathrm{H_{2}O}\), or \(\mathrm{HCl}\)) is eliminated at each link.
cards.why: Each monomer must have two reactive groups so that the chain can keep growing from both ends.

cards.q: Which pairs of monomers form (a) a polyester and (b) a polyamide? Which single type of monomer also forms a polyamide?
cards.a:
(a) A dicarboxylic acid and a diol.
(b) A dicarboxylic acid and a diamine.
Amino acids form polyamides on their own (proteins are polyamides).
cards.why: An amino acid has both an amine group and a carboxylic acid group in one molecule.

cards.q: Name and draw the linkage in (a) a polyester and (b) a polyamide.
cards.a:
(a) The ester link, \(\mathrm{-COO-}\).
(b) The amide link, \(\mathrm{-CONH-}\) (called a peptide link in proteins).
cards.why: These are the same groups found in simple esters and amides.

cards.q: Terylene (PET) is made from ethane-1,2-diol and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid. Draw its repeating unit.

figure.alt: Skeletal formulae of ethane-1,2-diol (HO–CH2–CH2–OH) and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid (a benzene ring with COOH groups at opposite corners).

cards.a: An ester link at each end of the benzene-1,4-dicarbonyl group, joined through O to \(\mathrm{CH_{2}CH_{2}}\). One water molecule is lost for each ester link.

answerFigure.alt: Repeating unit of Terylene (PET): an O, a C=O, a benzene ring joined at opposite corners, another C=O, an O, then CH2–CH2, all in square brackets with n.

cards.why: The acid loses OH from each \(\mathrm{COOH}\); the diol loses H from each OH.

cards.q: Write an equation for the formation of Terylene from its monomers.
cards.a: \(\mathrm{n\,HOOCC_{6}H_{4}COOH + n\,HOCH_{2}CH_{2}OH \rightarrow [{-}OCC_{6}H_{4}COOCH_{2}CH_{2}O{-}]_{n} + 2n\,H_{2}O}\)
cards.why: Each repeating unit contains two ester links, so \(2n\) water molecules are eliminated.

cards.q: Nylon-6,6 is made from hexanedioic acid and hexane-1,6-diamine. Draw its repeating unit.

figure.alt: Skeletal formulae of hexanedioic acid (a six-carbon chain with COOH at both ends) and hexane-1,6-diamine (a six-carbon chain with NH2 at both ends).

cards.a: \(\mathrm{-NH(CH_{2})_{6}NHCO(CH_{2})_{4}CO-}\): two amide links per repeating unit.

answerFigure.alt: Repeating unit of nylon-6,6: N–H, a chain of six CH2 groups, N–H, C=O, a chain of four CH2 groups, then C=O, all in square brackets with n.

cards.why: Count carbons: the acid gives a \(\mathrm{CO(CH_{2})_{4}CO}\) unit (6 C), the diamine \(\mathrm{NH(CH_{2})_{6}NH}\) (6 C).

cards.q: What do the two numbers in “nylon-6,6” mean?
cards.a: Each of the two monomers contains six carbon atoms: the diamine (first number) and the dicarboxylic acid (second number).
cards.why: Nylon-6,10, for example, is made from a six-carbon diamine and a ten-carbon dicarboxylic acid.

cards.q: Kevlar is made from benzene-1,4-diamine and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid. Draw its repeating unit.

figure.alt: Skeletal formulae of benzene-1,4-diamine (a benzene ring with NH2 at opposite corners) and benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid (a benzene ring with COOH at opposite corners).

cards.a: Two benzene rings in the chain, joined by amide links: –NH–ring–NH–CO–ring–CO–.

answerFigure.alt: Repeating unit of Kevlar: N–H, a benzene ring joined at opposite corners, N–H, C=O, a second benzene ring joined at opposite corners, then C=O, in square brackets with n.

cards.why: Kevlar is a polyamide like nylon, but its rigid flat rings let the chains line up closely.

cards.q: Give a typical use of Terylene (PET), nylon-6,6 and Kevlar.
cards.a:
Terylene: clothing fibres and plastic drinks bottles.
Nylon-6,6: ropes, fishing nets, clothing (tights).
Kevlar: bulletproof vests, helmets, and reinforcing tyres.
cards.why: Kevlar’s very strong hydrogen bonding between regular, rigid chains makes it about five times stronger than steel for the same mass.

cards.q: Nylon-6,6 can also be made from hexanedioyl dichloride instead of hexanedioic acid. Which small molecule is eliminated then, and why is this route used in the laboratory?
cards.a:
\(\mathrm{HCl}\) is eliminated instead of water.
Acyl chlorides are much more reactive than carboxylic acids, so the polymer forms quickly at room temperature.
cards.why: \(\mathrm{-COCl + H_{2}N- \rightarrow -CONH- + HCl}\)

cards.q: Describe how nylon-6,6 can be made in the laboratory by the “nylon rope trick”.
cards.a: Carefully pour a solution of hexanedioyl dichloride in an organic solvent (such as cyclohexane) on top of an aqueous solution of hexane-1,6-diamine. Nylon forms at the boundary between the two layers; grip it with tweezers and pull it out slowly as a continuous thread.
cards.why: The two monomers only meet at the interface, so the polymer forms there as fast as it is removed. Work in a fume cupboard: the acyl chloride is corrosive.

cards.q: Draw the repeating unit of the polyamide formed from 2-aminopropanoic acid (alanine) alone.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of 2-aminopropanoic acid: a carbon carrying an NH2 group, a methyl group and a COOH group.

cards.a: \(\mathrm{-NH-CH(CH_{3})-CO-}\): one amide (peptide) link per monomer.

answerFigure.alt: Repeating unit of the polyamide from 2-aminopropanoic acid: N–H, then a carbon carrying H and CH3, then C=O, in square brackets with n.

cards.why: One monomer has both groups, so the repeating unit comes from a single amino acid.

cards.q: Nylon-6 is made from a single monomer, 6-aminohexanoic acid, \(\mathrm{H_{2}N(CH_{2})_{5}COOH}\). Draw its repeating unit.

answerFigure.alt: Repeating unit of nylon-6: N–H, a chain of five CH2 groups, then C=O, in square brackets with n.

cards.why: Like an amino acid, the monomer has an amine group at one end and a carboxylic acid group at the other.

cards.q: Draw the repeating unit of the polyester formed from butanedioic acid and propane-1,3-diol.

figure.alt: Skeletal formulae of butanedioic acid (HOOC–CH2–CH2–COOH) and propane-1,3-diol (HO–CH2–CH2–CH2–OH).

answerFigure.alt: Repeating unit of the polyester from butanedioic acid and propane-1,3-diol: C=O, (CH2)2, C=O, O, (CH2)3, O, in square brackets with n.

cards.why: Check: the repeating unit has the atoms of one acid plus one diol, minus two molecules of water.

cards.q: Draw the repeating unit of the polyamide formed from butanedioic acid and ethane-1,2-diamine, \(\mathrm{H_{2}NCH_{2}CH_{2}NH_{2}}\).

answerFigure.alt: Repeating unit of the polyamide from butanedioic acid and ethane-1,2-diamine: C=O, (CH2)2, C=O, N–H, (CH2)2, N–H, in square brackets with n.

cards.why: Each link is \(\mathrm{-CONH-}\): the C=O comes from the acid and the N–H from the amine.

cards.q: Here is a section of a condensation polymer. Identify the type of polymer and draw the two monomers.

figure.alt: A section of a polymer chain: C=O, (CH2)2, C=O, O, (CH2)2, O, then C=O, (CH2)2, C=O, with bonds continuing at each end.

cards.a: A polyester. The monomers are butanedioic acid and ethane-1,2-diol.

answerFigure.alt: Skeletal formulae of butanedioic acid (HOOC–CH2–CH2–COOH) and ethane-1,2-diol (HO–CH2–CH2–OH).

cards.why: Break each ester link between C=O and O: add OH to each C=O and H to each O.

cards.q: This section of a condensation polymer contains a benzene ring. Identify the type of polymer and draw the two monomers.

figure.alt: A section of a polymer chain: N–H, a benzene ring joined at opposite corners, N–H, C=O, CH2, CH2, CH2, C=O, then N–H, with bonds continuing at each end.

cards.a: A polyamide. The monomers are benzene-1,4-diamine and pentanedioic acid.

answerFigure.alt: Skeletal formulae of benzene-1,4-diamine (a benzene ring with NH2 at opposite corners) and pentanedioic acid (HOOC–CH2–CH2–CH2–COOH).

cards.why: Break each amide link between C=O and N–H: add OH to the C=O and H to the N. The acid has five carbons, including both C=O carbons.

cards.q: A student draws the repeating unit of nylon-6,6 as \(\mathrm{-NH(CH_{2})_{6}NH-CO(CH_{2})_{4}COOH}\). What is wrong?
cards.a: The repeating unit must not keep the \(\mathrm{OH}\) (or a terminal \(\mathrm{H}\)): it ends in bonds that continue the chain, \(\mathrm{-NH(CH_{2})_{6}NHCO(CH_{2})_{4}CO-}\).
cards.why: The OH and H were lost as water when the links formed; only the chain ends of the whole molecule keep them.

cards.q: Give three differences between addition and condensation polymerisation.
cards.a:
Addition: monomers have a \(\mathrm{C{=}C}\); the polymer is the only product; often one monomer.
Condensation: monomers have two functional groups (such as \(\mathrm{-OH}\), \(\mathrm{-COOH}\), \(\mathrm{-NH_{2}}\)); a small molecule is also formed; often two different monomers.
cards.why: The chain of an addition polymer is all carbon; a condensation polymer chain contains ester or amide links.

cards.q: Explain why polyamides such as nylon and Kevlar are strong, with high melting points.
cards.a: Hydrogen bonds form between the chains.
marks: The amide link contains a \(\mathrm{N{-}H}\) group and a \(\mathrm{C{=}O}\) group.
Hydrogen bonds form between the \(\mathrm{H}\) of \(\mathrm{N{-}H}\) on one chain and a lone pair on the \(\mathrm{O}\) of \(\mathrm{C{=}O}\) on a neighbouring chain.
Hydrogen bonds are stronger than the van der Waals forces between poly(alkene) chains, so more energy is needed to separate the chains.

cards.q: Describe the intermolecular forces between polyester chains such as Terylene.
cards.a: Permanent dipole–dipole forces (and van der Waals forces), but no hydrogen bonds.
marks: The ester link has polar \(\mathrm{C{=}O}\) and \(\mathrm{C{-}O}\) bonds, so there are permanent dipole–dipole attractions between the chains.
There are van der Waals forces between the chains as well.
There is no \(\mathrm{H}\) bonded to \(\mathrm{O}\) or \(\mathrm{N}\) in the chain, so the chains cannot hydrogen bond to each other.

cards.q: A sample of nylon-6,6 has an average \(M_{\text{r}}\) of 45 200. The repeating unit is \(\mathrm{C_{12}H_{22}N_{2}O_{2}}\). Estimate the average number of repeating units in a chain. (\(A_{\text{r}}\): C 12.0, H 1.0, N 14.0, O 16.0)
cards.a: 200 repeating units
cards.why: The end groups of each chain are such a tiny part of the mass that they can be ignored.

cards.q: Poly(lactic acid), PLA, is a polyester made from one monomer, 2-hydroxypropanoic acid (lactic acid). Draw its repeating unit.

figure.alt: Skeletal formula of 2-hydroxypropanoic acid: a carbon carrying an OH group, a methyl group and a COOH group.

cards.a: \(\mathrm{-O-CH(CH_{3})-CO-}\)

answerFigure.alt: Repeating unit of poly(lactic acid): an O, then a carbon carrying H and CH3, then C=O, in square brackets with n.

cards.why: The monomer has an alcohol group and a carboxylic acid group, so it can form ester links at both ends.

cards.q: Explain why polyesters and polyamides can be hydrolysed, but poly(alkenes) cannot.
cards.a: Polyesters and polyamides have polar C=O groups that nucleophiles can attack; poly(alkenes) do not.
marks: Ester and amide links contain a polar \(\mathrm{C{=}O}\) bond, so the carbon is δ+.
Nucleophiles such as water or \(\mathrm{OH^{-}}\) attack the δ+ carbon and the link breaks (hydrolysis).
Poly(alkenes) have only non-polar \(\mathrm{C{-}C}\) and \(\mathrm{C{-}H}\) bonds, so there is no δ+ carbon to attack.

cards.q: Terylene is heated with aqueous sodium hydroxide. Name the two organic products.
cards.a: Ethane-1,2-diol and sodium benzene-1,4-dicarboxylate (the salt of the acid).

answerFigure.alt: Products of alkaline hydrolysis: ethane-1,2-diol, and the benzene-1,4-dicarboxylate ion: a benzene ring with a COO minus group at opposite corners (its sodium salt forms).

cards.why: In alkali the acid formed is neutralised, so its salt is formed; acid hydrolysis would give benzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid itself.

cards.q: Nylon-6,6 is heated with hydrochloric acid. Give the products.
cards.a: Hexanedioic acid, \(\mathrm{HOOC(CH_{2})_{4}COOH}\), and the salt hexane-1,6-diammonium chloride, \(\mathrm{ClH_{3}N(CH_{2})_{6}NH_{3}Cl}\).
cards.why: The amine groups formed are basic, so in acid they are protonated to \(\mathrm{-NH_{3}^{+}}\). With NaOH instead, you get the diamine and sodium hexanedioate.

cards.q: What is meant by a biodegradable polymer?
cards.a: A polymer that can be broken down by microorganisms (bacteria and fungi) in the environment into small molecules such as carbon dioxide and water.
cards.why: Polyesters and polyamides can be hydrolysed, so they are biodegradable; poly(alkenes) are not.

cards.q: True or false: poly(ethene) carrier bags rot away in a few months because microorganisms digest them.
cards.a: False. Poly(alkenes) are not biodegradable; they can last for hundreds of years.
cards.why: Microorganisms have no way to break the strong non-polar C–C and C–H bonds. This is why discarded bags block drains and harm animals.

cards.q: Give four ways of dealing with waste polymers.
cards.a: Landfill; incineration (to release energy); recycling (melting and remoulding); use as a feedstock, for example cracking to make new chemicals.
cards.why: Waste polymers must first be sorted into specific types for recycling or feedstock use.

cards.q: Give the advantages and disadvantages of disposing of waste polymers in landfill.
cards.a: Cheap and easy, but wasteful and damaging.
marks: Advantage: cheap and simple; no sorting is needed.
Disadvantage: takes up a lot of land; poly(alkenes) do not break down, so they stay for centuries.
Disadvantage: the energy and crude oil locked in the polymer are wasted.
Disadvantage: toxic additives can leach into the soil and water.

cards.q: Give the advantages and disadvantages of incinerating waste polymers.
cards.a: Energy is recovered, but harmful gases are formed.
marks: Advantage: the energy released can generate electricity or heat buildings.
Advantage: the volume of waste going to landfill is greatly reduced.
Disadvantage: \(\mathrm{CO_{2}}\), a greenhouse gas, is released.
Disadvantage: toxic gases can form, such as \(\mathrm{HCl}\) from PVC and \(\mathrm{CO}\) from incomplete combustion.

cards.q: How do chemists remove acidic gases such as hydrogen chloride from the waste gases of a plastics incinerator?
cards.a:
Pass the gases through a base, such as calcium oxide or calcium carbonate (a “scrubber”), which neutralises the acid:
\(\mathrm{CaO + 2HCl \rightarrow CaCl_{2} + H_{2}O}\)
cards.why: \(\mathrm{HCl}\) comes from chlorine-containing polymers such as PVC; it would otherwise form acid rain.

cards.q: True or false: PVC is a hydrocarbon, so burning it gives only carbon dioxide and water.
cards.a: False. PVC contains chlorine, so burning it also forms hydrogen chloride (and other toxic chlorine compounds).
cards.why: The repeating unit is \(\mathrm{-CH_{2}CHCl-}\). A hydrocarbon contains only carbon and hydrogen.

cards.q: Give the advantages and disadvantages of recycling waste polymers.
cards.a: Saves resources, but needs careful sorting and the quality can fall.
marks: Advantage: saves crude oil, which is a finite resource, and the energy needed to make new polymer.
Advantage: less waste goes to landfill, and less CO₂ is produced than by incineration.
Disadvantage: polymers must be collected and sorted into types, which is expensive and labour-intensive.
Disadvantage: the polymer can only be recycled a limited number of times, as its quality falls.

cards.q: What is meant by using waste polymers as a feedstock?
cards.a: Sorted waste polymer is broken down, for example by cracking, into smaller molecules such as alkenes, which are then used to make new polymers and other chemicals.
cards.why: It recovers the raw materials, not just the energy, from the waste.

cards.q: How can chemists help make the use of polymers more sustainable over the whole life cycle of a product?
cards.a: By looking at the energy and resources used at every stage: making the monomer from crude oil or from renewable plants, manufacturing, using, and disposing of the product. Examples: lighter packaging that needs less polymer, making monomers from renewable sources, designing products that are easy to recycle, and recovering energy or feedstock at the end.
cards.why: A life-cycle assessment compares products from “cradle to grave”, not just at one stage.

cards.q: Give two ways chemists have developed polymers that cause fewer disposal problems.
cards.a:
Biodegradable polymers such as poly(lactic acid), made from plant starch (maize, cassava or sugar cane), which microorganisms can break down.
Photodegradable polymers, which contain groups that absorb light and weaken the chains.
cards.why: Plant-based monomers are also renewable, unlike monomers from crude oil.

cards.q: True or false: a biodegradable polymer causes no problems once it is buried in landfill.
cards.a: False. Deep in landfill there is little oxygen, light or moisture, so it breaks down very slowly, and anaerobic breakdown can release methane, a greenhouse gas.
cards.why: Biodegradable polymers break down best in industrial composting, which needs separate collection.

cards.q: Rwanda and Kenya have banned single-use plastic carrier bags. Using chemistry, explain why such bans were introduced.
cards.a: The bags are poly(ethene), which is not biodegradable: discarded bags build up in the environment, block drains (adding to flooding), and harm livestock and marine life. Burning them in open fires releases toxic gases.
cards.why: Policies that reduce use, encourage reuse or switch to biodegradable materials tackle the problem at the start of the life cycle.
